questions.prompt: Which phase feeds directly back into Preparation, closing the IR lifecycle into a loop rather than a straight line?
questions.explanation: Lessons Learned is specifically about identifying what would have made Preparation better for the next incident — that's what closes the loop instead of leaving it a one-way line.

questions.prompt: A responder wants to immediately delete a malicious scheduled task the moment it's found, before finishing the search for other persistence mechanisms. What's the concern with doing that right away?
options: Deleting a scheduled task requires domain admin rights
It risks tipping off the attacker before containment is confirmed and the rest of their footholds are found
Scheduled tasks can't actually be deleted while a system is live
It violates chain-of-custody requirements in every case
questions.explanation: This is the Containment-before-Eradication sequencing problem: loud eradication actions taken before containment is solid can alert an attacker who still has other access, causing them to accelerate or go quieter.

questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between short-term and long-term Containment?
options: There is no real difference — it's one continuous step
Short-term buys time (isolate, disable, block); long-term restores stable operation while eradication is planned
Short-term applies only to cloud incidents, long-term only to on-prem
Long-term containment always happens before short-term
questions.explanation: Short-term containment is about stopping active damage fast. Long-term containment is about reaching a stable state that holds while the eradication plan is actually built — conflating the two is what leads to premature eradication.

questions.prompt: Why is Preparation often the easiest phase to under-invest in?
options: It's the most expensive phase to fund
It's invisible when done well — there's no incident happening to show its value in the moment
It only matters for organizations larger than 500 employees
It's not actually part of most published IR frameworks
questions.explanation: Good preparation (logging, baselines, an accurate asset inventory) has no visible payoff until an incident happens — which makes it easy to deprioritize against work with more immediate, visible results.
